title: Review: Forces and momentum; Work, energy and power
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: A.3#c15 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; A.3#c04 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; A.2#c13 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; A.2#c04 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: A.2#q30, A.2#q38, A.2#q32, A.3#q01, A.3#q03, A.3#q04, A.3#q08, A.2#q29, A.2#q31, A.2#q39, A.3#q02, A.3#q05. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Power (P)
items.clue: The rate at which work is done.

items.label: Joule (J)
items.clue: The SI unit of work and of energy.

items.label: Tension, T
items.clue: The pulling force exerted by a string, rope, cable or rod on a body attached to it, directed along the string away from the body.

items.label: Translational equilibrium
items.clue: The state of a body on which the resultant force is zero, so that by Newton's first law it is at rest or moving with constant velocity.

questions.stem: A small ball of mass 0.30 kg on a string of length 0.60 m swings as a pendulum in a vertical plane. As it passes through its lowest point its speed is 2.8 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the tension in the string at this point?
questions.explanation: At the lowest point the centre of the circle is above the ball. The resultant force towards the centre is T − mg = mv²/r, so T = 0.30 × 9.8 + 0.30 × 2.8²/0.60 = 2.9 + 3.9 = 6.9 N.

questions.stem: A car moves around a horizontal circular track and its speed is increasing. Which statement about the resultant force on the car is correct?

options.text: It points directly towards the centre, whatever the speed of the car is doing.
It points directly along the direction of motion, because the car is speeding up.
It is directed away from the centre, as the car tends to slide outwards.
It has a component towards the centre and a component along the direction of motion.

questions.explanation: The centripetal component, mv²/r, changes the direction of the velocity; a tangential component, along the velocity, changes its magnitude. Both are needed when a body moves in a circle with increasing speed, so the resultant points between the centre and the tangent.

questions.stem: A bicycle wheel of diameter 0.700 m rotates at a steady rate about a fixed axle, making one complete revolution every 0.250 s. What is the linear speed of a point on the rim of the wheel?
A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 2.0 m onto a hard floor and rebounds to a height of 1.5 m. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement correctly accounts for the energy?

options.text: The total is unchanged; a quarter of the ball's mechanical energy became internal energy and sound.
Energy was not conserved in the bounce, because a quarter of the ball's energy was used up and destroyed.
Mechanical energy is conserved, so the missing quarter is still stored as elastic potential energy in the ball.
The missing quarter of the ball's energy was changed into the force that the floor exerted on the ball.

questions.stem: Work done and energy are both measured in joules. Which statement correctly defines one joule of work done?

options.text: The work done when a force of 1 N acts on a body for a time of 1 s, whether or not the body moves at all.
The work done when a force of 1 N moves its point of application 1 m in the direction of the force.
The work done when a force of 1 N acts on a body that moves 1 m in any direction relative to that force.
The energy that a force of 1 N contains, whatever body it acts on or however it moves.

questions.explanation: W = Fs cos θ = 1 N × 1 m × cos 0° = 1 N m = 1 J. Work and energy share the joule because the work done by a force IS the energy it transfers.

questions.stem: A student draws a Sankey diagram for an electric motor. The input arrow is 50 mm wide and represents 100 J of electrical energy. Only two output arrows are drawn: one 20 mm wide for work done lifting a load, and one 25 mm wide for thermal energy transferred to the surroundings. Which statement about the diagram is correct?

options.text: An arrow is missing, but it only represents 5 J, as 1 mm of width stands for 1 J.
No arrow is missing; the other 10 J was used up inside the motor and is gone.
The lifting arrow should be widest, as it shows the motor's useful output.
An arrow 5 mm wide is missing; it represents 10 J, since the outputs must total 100 J.

questions.stem: A trolley moves 4.0 m in a straight line. One of the forces acting on it is a constant 20 N force directed at 120° to the trolley's displacement. How much work does this force do on the trolley?
questions.explanation: W = Fs cos θ = 20 × 4.0 × cos 120° = 80 × (−0.50) = −40 J. The force has a component opposite to the displacement, so it transfers energy away from the trolley.

questions.stem: A car travels at constant speed around a bend on a flat horizontal road; its path is part of a horizontal circle. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the horizontal forces on the car is correct?

options.text: Friction from the road acts towards the centre and is the resultant force.
Friction acts towards the centre and is balanced by a centrifugal force.
Friction and a separate centripetal force both act towards the centre.
A forward driving force along the bend is the resultant force on the car.

questions.explanation: On a flat road the only horizontal force towards the centre is friction between the tyres and the road. With air resistance negligible, no force is needed along the path at constant speed, so this friction is the resultant force and provides the centripetal force mv²/r.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides around a flat circular track at a constant speed of 8.0 m s⁻¹. Which statement about her motion is correct?

options.text: Her velocity is constant, so the resultant force acting on her is zero.
Her velocity changes, so a resultant force acts towards the centre.
A resultant force acts on her outwards, away from the centre of the track.
A resultant force acts on her forwards, along her direction of motion.

questions.explanation: Velocity is a vector. Her speed is constant but the direction of her velocity changes continuously, so she accelerates towards the centre and, by Newton's second law, a resultant force acts towards the centre.

questions.stem: A disc rotates at a steady rate about its centre, completing 3.0 revolutions in 2.0 s. A mark on the disc is 0.15 m from the centre. What is the angular velocity of the disc?

options.text: 9.4 rad s⁻¹
1.5 rad s⁻¹
540 rad s⁻¹
1.4 rad s⁻¹

questions.explanation: The disc makes 1.5 revolutions per second, and each revolution is 2π rad, so ω = 2π × 1.5 = 9.4 rad s⁻¹. Equivalently T = 2.0/3.0 s and ω = 2π/T.

questions.stem: A weightlifter holds a barbell stationary above her head for 4.0 s. How much work does she do on the barbell during these 4.0 s?

options.text: A large amount, because holding the heavy barbell up takes a great deal of effort.
Her upward force multiplied by the 4.0 s for which she holds it up.
An amount equal to the gravitational potential energy of the barbell.
None, because the barbell does not move, so no energy is transferred to it.

questions.explanation: Work is done on a body only when the force moves its point of application: W = Fs cos θ with s = 0 gives W = 0. The barbell's energy does not change while it is held still. Her muscles do transfer chemical energy to internal energy in her body, which is why she tires, but none of this goes to the barbell.

questions.stem: Which statement is true of every correctly drawn Sankey diagram?

options.text: The output arrows are narrower in total than the input, as energy is used up.
The longest arrow on the diagram represents the largest transfer of energy.
The widths of the output arrows add up to the width of the input arrow.
The arrow for the useful output is wider than any arrow for wasted energy.

questions.explanation: Width represents energy (or power) to scale, and energy is conserved, so the total of the outputs, useful and wasted, equals the input. This is what a Sankey diagram shows at a glance.
